hello.note: To several people or to show respect to an elder: sanibonani. Reply: yebo, sawubona.

goodbye.note: Said by the one leaving. To someone who is leaving: hamba kahle.

please.note: Before what you ask for, drop -ya-: ngicela amanzi (water, please).

thank_you.note: Ngiyabonga kakhulu: thank you very much. Siyabonga (we thank you) is also very common.

youre_welcome.note: There is no fixed reply; kulungile (it's fine) is usual. The calque wamukelekile is heard too.

yes.note: Also the standard reply to sawubona. Casual: ehe.

no.note: The c is a click: the 'tsk' sound, tongue behind the front teeth.

sorry.note: The x is a click, like urging on a horse. For a small slip, uxolo is enough.

excuse_me.note: Add baba (to a man) or mama (to a woman) to sound respectful: uxolo, baba.

good_morning.note: Asks how you woke up. Reply: ngivuke kahle. Sawubona also works at any hour.

how_are_you.note: To an elder or several people: ninjani? Casual: kunjani? (how's it going?)

im_fine.note: Also: ngikhona (I'm here). Then ask back: wena unjani?

whats_your_name.note: In speech often shortened to: ubani igama lakho?

my_name_is.note: Ngu- joins the name: igama lami nguThabo. Also common: nginguThabo (I'm Thabo).

where_from.note: Can also mean 'where have you just come from?'. Ungowaphi? asks only about origin.

im_from.note: The place joins the e-: ngivela eJalimane (from Germany). A few places take kwa- instead.

speak_english.note: Also common: uyasazi isiNgisi? (do you know English?)

dont_understand.note: Literally 'I don't hear', the everyday way to say it. Angizwa isiZulu: I don't understand Zulu.

where.note: Usually a suffix: uyaphi? (where are you going?), iphi? (where is it?)

what.note: Usually a suffix: ufunani? (what do you want?). 'What did you say?': uthini?

how_much.note: Also: yimalini? (how much money is it?)

what_time.note: Just as common: sithini isikhathi? (literally 'what does the time say?')

what_means.note: For a single word: leli gama lisho ukuthini?

one.note: The counting form. In daily life prices and times are often said in English.

two.note: With a noun it agrees: izinto ezimbili (two things).

three.note: With a noun it agrees: abantu abathathu (three people).

five.note: hl is like Welsh ll: breathe out past the side of the tongue.

six.note: Literally 'thumb': counting on the fingers moves on to the second hand.

bill_please.note: Or: ngicela ukukhokha (I'd like to pay).

delicious.note: Kumnandi kakhulu!: really delicious. Mnandi also means nice or fun.

left.note: The x is a click. Turn left: jika ngakwesokunxele.

right.note: From -dla, to eat: the side of the hand you eat with.

straight_ahead.note: Both q's are clicks. Phambili means ahead, forward.

stop_here.note: In a minibus taxi: ngiyehla lapha (I'm getting off here).

want_to_go.note: The place joins the e-: ngifuna ukuya eThekwini (to Durban).

id_like_this.note: More direct: ngifuna lokhu (I want this).

open.note: Shop signs in South Africa are usually in English.

big.note: Agrees with the noun: indlu enkulu (a big house).

small.note: Agrees with the noun: indlu encane (a small house).

good_evening.note: Zulu has no set evening greeting: sawubona is used at any hour.

allergic.note: Before an English name add a hyphen: ngine-aleji ku-penicillin.

be_careful.note: The q is a loud pop of the tongue. To several people: qaphelani!

i_like_it.note: Said to a person it means 'I love you'. It changes with the noun: ngiyayithanda for ingubo (dress).

dont_like_it.note: Changes with the noun like ngiyakuthanda: angiyithandi.

welcome.note: To several guests: namukelekile! Hosts also say ngena (come in).

my_family.note: Possessives follow the noun and agree with it: umama wami (my mother), ubaba wami (my father).

mother.note: Also how you respectfully address any older woman: mama.

father.note: Also how you respectfully address any older man: baba.

brother.note: Literally 'our brother', the usual way to say 'my brother'. An older brother is often called ubhuti.

sister.note: Literally 'our sister', the usual way to say 'my sister'. An older sister is often called usisi.

child.note: Plural: izingane. Son: indodana; daughter: indodakazi.

friend.note: Same word for a man or a woman. Plural: abangane. My friend: umngane wami.

this_is_my_friend.note: Same for a male or female friend. Lo means 'this person'.

are_you_married.note: Same for a man or a woman. Answers: ngishadile (I'm married), angishadile (I'm not).

have_children.note: Answers: nginezingane ezimbili (I have two), anginazo (I have none).

monday.note: Days take a capital after the u-. On Monday: ngoMsombuluko.

saturday.note: Gq is the q click made deeper, with voice. On Saturday: ngoMgqibelo.

sunday.note: Isonto also means 'week' and 'church'. On Sunday: ngeSonto.

weekend.note: Literally 'end of the week'. At the weekend: ngempelasonto. Many simply say i-weekend.

next_week.note: Elizayo: 'that is coming'. Last week: ngesonto eledlule.

eleven.note: Literally 'ten and one'. Prices, ages and times are often said in English.

twenty.note: Literally 'two tens': amashumi is the plural of ishumi.

thirty.note: Literally 'three tens'. Thirty-five: amashumi amathathu nanhlanu.

years_old.note: With English numbers: ngineminyaka engu-25. Before amashumi: engamashumi amabili (20).

red.note: Colours agree with the noun: imoto ebomvu (a red car).

blue.note: Literally 'green-blue like the sky'. Luhlaza alone covers both colours.

green.note: Literally 'green-blue like grass'. In context luhlaza alone is enough.

yellow.note: Agrees like the other colours: imbali ephuzi (a yellow flower).

black.note: Mnyama also means dark: kumnyama (it's dark).

white.note: The hl is breathed out past the side of the tongue, as in kuhlanu (five).

what_colour.note: Answer with the colour: imoto ibomvu (the car is red).

this_one.note: Changes with the noun: lesi for isinkwa (bread), leli for ihembe (shirt).

that_one.note: Further off, over there: leya. Changes with the noun like lena: leso, lelo.

another_one.note: Enye agrees with the noun: ngicela esinye for isinkwa (bread).

its_raining.note: Fuller: izulu liyana. Izulu means sky, weather and heaven.

its_sunny.note: Ilanga also means 'day'. Also: libalele (the sun is blazing hot).

its_windy.note: Literally 'there is wind'. Umoya also means air and spirit.

weather_today.note: On the news the weather is isimo sezulu.

beautiful_day.note: Literally 'the weather is beautiful today'. Usuku oluhle: a beautiful day.

have_reservation.note: Literally 'I have booked'. Then give your name: igama lami nguThabo.

room.note: Any room of a house too. Bedroom: ikamelo lokulala.

luggage.note: Singular: umthwalo (a load, one piece of luggage). A bag: isikhwama.

wifi_password.note: Ithini: 'what does it say?', as in sithini isikhathi?

check_out_time.note: Literally 'at what time must I leave?'. For a group: kufanele siphume.

map.note: The formal, school word is ibalazwe.

next_train.note: Sihamba: it leaves. To ask when it arrives: sifika nini?

is_this_seat_free.note: Literally 'is someone sitting here?', so cha (no) means it's free.

what_do_you_do.note: Also common: usebenzaphi? (where do you work?)

i_work_in.note: A place joins the e-: ngisebenza ebhange (at a bank). A field takes kwe-: kwezempilo (in health).

im_student.note: Same for a man or a woman. At university: ngifunda enyuvesi.

office.note: The hh is a breathy, voiced h. At the office: ehhovisi.

day_off.note: Literally 'day of rest'. I'm off today: angisebenzi namuhla.

colleague.note: Literally 'our peer'; same for a man or a woman. Plural: ozakwethu.

good_job.note: To several people: nenze kahle! Also: halala!

table_for_two.note: As a couple, sicela (we ask) is just as natural.

what_recommend.note: Casual: yini emnandi lapha? (what's good here?)

not_spicy.note: Literally 'please don't add chilli'. Spicy food 'burns': kuyashisa.

vegetarian_food.note: Literally 'food without meat'. I'm vegetarian: angiyidli inyama.

more_water.note: Amanye agrees with amanzi. More bread: ngicela esinye isinkwa.

no_sugar.note: With milk: nobisi. Without milk: ngaphandle kobisi.

im_full.note: Ngisuthi, ngiyabonga is the polite way to turn down more food.

takeaway.note: Literally 'I'd like to go with it'. Many simply say: ngicela i-takeaway.

it_was_delicious.note: Be- puts it in the past: kumnandi, bekumnandi.

keep_change.note: Zigcinele: 'keep it for yourself'. Also very common: ushintshi ngowakho (the change is yours).

stomach.note: Also the belly. My stomach hurts: ngiphethwe yisisu.

head_hurts.note: Literally 'the head has hold of me'. Also: ikhanda lami libuhlungu.

have_fever.note: Umkhuhlane also covers flu. Also: umzimba wami uyashisa (my body is hot).

medicine.note: Also means tree and traditional medicine. Pills: amaphilisi.

call_ambulance.note: In South Africa dial 10177, or 112 from a cellphone.

feel_better.note: Se- adds 'now, already': ngizizwa (I feel), sengizizwa. Also: sengiphilile (I'm well now).

get_well.note: Literally 'recover quickly'. To several people: nilulame ngokushesha!

lets_meet.note: Also: masihlangane. Asibonane (let's see each other) is common too.

are_you_free.note: Also: uzotholakala kusasa? (will you be available?)

call_me.note: Fuller: ngicela ungishayele ucingo. Among friends: ngishayele.

have_nice_day.note: To several people: nibe nosuku oluhle!

good_luck.note: Literally 'I wish you luck'. Shorter, casual: inhlanhla enhle!

thanks_a_lot.note: Siyabonga kakhulu (we thank you) is just as common and sounds warm.

miss_you.note: Literally 'I remember you'. To several people: ngiyanikhumbula.
